claims.text: The anomalously high yield strength of refractory HEAs is mainly governed by inherent lattice distortions.
The relatively preserved high-temperature elastic modulus of refractory HEAs is mainly governed by inherent lattice distortions.
Atomic size mismatch produces inherent lattice distortions in refractory HEAs.
Lattice distortions create localized internal stress fields.
Localized distortion-induced stress fields stabilize dislocation structures or networks.
Distortion-induced internal stress fields hinder dislocation motion during high-temperature deformation.
Lattice distortions reduce thermal softening of the elastic modulus at high temperatures.
Compositional tuning that reduces elemental size mismatch will minimize lattice distortion while otherwise similar processing is maintained.
Alloys with less lattice distortion will be governed more strongly by conventional thermal softening and creep behavior.
The high-distortion refractory HEA will have higher high-temperature yield strength than an identically processed, reduced-distortion refractory HEA.
The high-distortion refractory HEA will exhibit a more gradual decrease in elastic modulus with increasing temperature than the reduced-distortion baseline.
In-situ diffraction will reveal more pronounced localized strain fields in the high-distortion alloy than in the reduced-distortion baseline.
The localized strain fields observed by diffraction will correlate with the imposed difference in lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase, disordered BCC refractory HEAs over the tested range of 500–1200 °C.
Precipitation or phase separation may cause behavior to deviate from the proposed lattice-distortion mechanism.
Oxidation may cause behavior to deviate from the proposed mechanism.
Grain boundaries, minor precipitates, and processing variations may overlap with lattice-distortion effects and alter the quantitative strength and modulus differences.
